result: The Million Death Study (MDS) captured 27,000 child deaths (13,490 girls and 13,007 boys aged 1–59 months) from 1.3 million households surveyed from 2005 to 2013 using verbal autopsy methods with physician coding.
evaluation: Claims C3, C26, and C122-C129 provide comprehensive documentation of the MDS methodology, sample size, and data collection procedures. The study design is well-described with appropriate quality assurance measures including dual physician coding and adjudication processes, supporting the validity of the data source.

result: Of 1,638 measles deaths identified, 79% occurred in rural areas, 73% in campaign states, 59% at ages 12–59 months, and 57% in girls. Prior to campaign launch, 76% of measles deaths were concentrated in campaign states, which decreased to 59% following campaign launch.
evaluation: Claims C27-C32 and C38-C41 provide consistent descriptive statistics from the study data showing the distribution of measles deaths by geography, age, and sex. The shift in geographic distribution from pre- to post-campaign periods is clearly documented and supports the subsequent impact analysis.

result: Measles mortality rates fell 27% in campaign states versus 11% in non-campaign states following campaign launch. The average annual rate reduction (AARR) accelerated from 12% overall to 22% post-campaign, with the highest declines in campaign states (15%) and specifically in Madhya Pradesh (20%), Uttar Pradesh (19%), Rajasthan (17%), Chhattisgarh (17%), and Gujarat (14%).
evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C43-C51 present consistent quantitative findings showing differential mortality declines between campaign and non-campaign states. The state-level AARR data (Table 2) provides granular evidence supporting the overall national trends, with confidence intervals indicating statistical significance for key states.

result: Interrupted time series analysis showed that measles mortality rates in campaign states declined significantly following campaign launch (slope change: -0.164, 95% CI -0.320 to -0.008, p=0.040) when compared to control deaths, while non-campaign states showed no significant change. The declines were specific to measles deaths, with no significant changes observed for pneumonia or diarrhea deaths.
evaluation: Claims C52 and C59-C67 present the core interrupted time series findings with appropriate statistical methods (C137-C140). The use of control deaths (injuries, congenital anomalies, non-communicable diseases) that were unaffected by measles vaccination and had comparable pre-intervention trends (p=0.9) strengthens the causal inference. The specificity to measles deaths (C66-C67) supports that the effect was due to the campaign rather than general improvements in child health.

result: The interrupted time series design controlled for potential confounding by using control deaths from conditions unaffected by measles vaccination. No other mass public health interventions targeted the 1-59 month age group during the study period. The intervention year was set to 2009 to account for a temporary increase in measles mortality that may have reflected expanded surveillance.
evaluation: Claims C53-C58 and C116-C117 address key methodological considerations for causal inference. The absence of other interventions (C53) and the biological plausibility of control group selection (C54-C55) strengthen the attribution of observed effects to the measles campaign. The adjustment for surveillance expansion in 2009 (C56-C58) demonstrates appropriate handling of potential measurement artifacts.

result: Girls saw steeper declines in measles mortality than boys in campaign states, though the direction of effect was similar in both sexes. Girls had higher odds of measles mortality (OR 1.3, 99% CI 1.1–1.5) than boys, with higher excess measles mortality risk distributed more widely in girls than boys in campaign states. Despite narrowing of the girl-boy gap, mortality remains higher in girls.
evaluation: Claims C6, C68-C71, C82-C84, and C112-C115 consistently document sex-specific patterns in measles mortality and campaign impact. The multilevel regression analysis (C82) provides statistical evidence for higher baseline risk in girls, while the interrupted time series (C68) and geographic analysis (C83-C84) demonstrate differential campaign impact. The persistence of higher mortality in girls despite campaign success (C113-C114) is supported by citations to prior work on gender disparities in India (C115).

result: Declines in mortality were specific to measles deaths, with no significant changes in slope for pneumonia and diarrhea deaths following campaign launch. The lack of effect in pneumonia deaths may be due to measles contributing a smaller etiologic fraction than other viral, bacterial, or fungal agents.
evaluation: Claims C7, C66-C67 provide consistent evidence from interrupted time series analysis that the mortality declines were specific to measles rather than reflecting general improvements in child health. The speculative explanation for lack of pneumonia effect (C118) is appropriately qualified and supported by citation to submitted work, though this remains a hypothesis requiring further investigation.

result: Multilevel logistic regression analysis showed that children living in a campaign district had lower measles mortality risk (OR 0.6, 99% CI 0.4–0.8), as did children born in 2009 or later (OR 0.8, 99% CI 0.7–0.9). The odds of measles mortality were higher at 12–59 months (OR 1.5, 99% CI 1.3–1.7) than at ages 1–11 months.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C81 present findings from multilevel logistic regression (C141-C143) that complement the interrupted time series analysis. The hierarchical structure accounting for clustering at district and state levels is appropriate for the data structure. The findings are internally consistent with the time series results and provide individual-level evidence for campaign effectiveness.

result: The campaign averted 41,000–56,000 deaths (median 48,500) during 2010–2013, representing 39–57% of expected deaths nationally. The majority of deaths averted were in campaign states (median 41,000), with similar numbers among girls (median 18,500) and boys (median 22,500).
evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C85-C86 present mortality impact estimates derived from the interrupted time series models. The range reflects sensitivity to case definitions (broad vs. narrow), which is appropriate. However, the uncertainty bounds may be underestimated as they don't fully account for all sources of uncertainty in the extrapolation from observed trends to counterfactual scenarios. The estimates are consistent with prior modeling studies (C89), lending external validity.

result: National measles immunization coverage improved from 2002 to 2014, particularly in campaign states, with a significant increase in campaign states relative to non-campaign states concurrent with campaign launch (difference-in-difference estimate 16.9%, p=0.0000009). Other health indicators showed increases over time but did not differ significantly between campaign and non-campaign states.
evaluation: Claims C77-C80 and C119-C120 provide evidence from national survey data (C144) that measles vaccination coverage increased differentially in campaign states, supporting the mechanism for observed mortality declines. The difference-in-difference analysis appropriately controls for secular trends. The lack of differential change in other health indicators (C79-C80) strengthens the inference that mortality declines were specifically due to the measles campaign rather than general health system improvements.

result: The proportion of measles deaths reporting at least one dose of measles vaccine rose modestly in campaign states (34% to 47%) but was mostly unchanged in non-campaign states (48% to 51%). The proportion vaccinated did not differ across case definitions, suggesting physician assignment of deaths was not unduly biased by vaccination history.
evaluation: Claims C33-C36 address potential bias in case ascertainment from verbal autopsy. The finding that vaccination proportions were similar across different case definitions (C35-C36) provides evidence against systematic bias where physicians might be less likely to assign measles as cause of death if the child was vaccinated. This supports the validity of the verbal autopsy approach for measuring measles mortality.

result: Alternative definitions of measles cases using one or both physicians assigning measles as the underlying cause of death yielded similar results. Moving the intervention year to 2010 resulted in a non-significant slope change but a significant decrease in level of measles mortality (-1.05, 95% CI -1.50 to -0.61).
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 present sensitivity analyses that test the robustness of findings to different case definitions and intervention timing. The consistency across case definitions (C72-C73) strengthens confidence in the main findings. The sensitivity to intervention year choice (C74-C75) is appropriately acknowledged, with the level change when using 2010 potentially reflecting actual vaccine delivery timing. These analyses demonstrate appropriate attention to methodological uncertainties.

result: Annual measles deaths at ages 1–59 months fell from 62,000 to 24,000 from 2005 to 2013. Age distributions did not differ greatly between pre-campaign and post-campaign periods.
evaluation: Claims C37 and C42 provide descriptive statistics on overall mortality trends and age distribution stability. These findings are well-supported by the data presented in Figure 1 and supplements. The stability of age distributions (C42) is important for ruling out demographic shifts as an explanation for observed mortality changes.

result: The authors conclude that elimination of measles deaths in India is feasible based on observed drastic declines. They compare their direct estimates with WHO modeled estimates and suggest substantial downward revisions are needed. They discuss challenges to elimination including high infectivity, suboptimal coverage, and the need for regular supplementary immunization activities.
evaluation: Claims C12 and C87-C109 present discussion and interpretation of findings in the context of measles elimination goals. While the observed mortality declines are substantial and well-documented, the conclusion that elimination is "feasible" (C12) is speculative and not directly tested. The comparison with WHO estimates (C91-C96) raises important questions about measurement but the discrepancies are not fully resolved. The discussion of elimination challenges (C99-C108) appropriately acknowledges barriers, and the inference about herd immunity (C109) is appropriately qualified as speculative. Overall, these claims represent reasonable interpretation but go beyond what the data directly demonstrate.

result: The authors establish the context that India comprises much of global childhood measles mortality, describe the 2010 mass second-dose measles immunization campaign implementation, and justify the use of interrupted time series as a robust quasi-experimental evaluation method given that randomized trials were not practical.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C13-C25 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to prior literature and government policy documents. The justification for the study design (C22-C25) is well-reasoned given the constraints of evaluating a national policy rollout. These claims establish the rationale and methodological approach for the study.

result: Since 2013, 11 states in India have implemented laboratory-confirmed measles surveillance, which provides sero-epidemiological data to facilitate diagnoses, detect suspected cases, and sequence circulating measles genotypes.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 describe surveillance infrastructure developments supported by appropriate citations. This contextual information is relevant for understanding the evolving capacity for measles monitoring in India but is not a primary finding of the current study.

result: The analysis focused on children aged 1–59 months who comprised 84% of measles deaths in the campaign target age group. Mortality rates were calculated using three-year moving averages weighted by sampling probabilities, applied to UN population estimates, and analyzed using log-transformed rates in six-month periods. Geographic analysis used generalized linear geostatistical models.
evaluation: Claims C130-C136 and C145-C147 describe analytical methods that are appropriate for the data structure and research questions. The focus on 1-59 months (C130-C131) is justified by the concentration of deaths in this age group. The use of moving averages, weighting, and log transformation (C132-C136) are standard approaches for mortality rate analysis. Software versions are specified (C146-C147), supporting reproducibility.
